To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
telomeres and ribosomal genes are organized in 3‐D in plant nuclei, and that this is the first demonstration of this in plants.
the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) and the telomeric DNA in plant nuclei are located in distinct domains.

(i) telomeres are located around the nuclear peripheries in interphase nuclei of plant cells, (ii) the ribosomal genes exist in discrete, three‐dimensional domains, and (iii) the ribosomal domains are located in the central regions of the nucleus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the 3‐ D organization of the interphase nucleus in plants and with the use of in‐situ techniques to investigate this.
understanding the organization of DNA in the nucleus of higher eukaryotes and the role of this organization in nuclear functions such as transcription, DNA replication and recombination.
the development of a new approach to study the 3‐dimensional organization of interphase plant nuclei.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in plants, there is evidence that telomeres cluster in the periphery of the nucleus and that the ribosome DNA is localized in 3‐D clusters.
the 3‐dimensional organization of the plant nucleus is not random, but rather that it is organized into distinct domains.
the 3‐dimensional arrangement of DNA sequences in plant nuclei is not random and is likely to have a functional basis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the telomeres and rDNA genes of P. sativum are not randomly distributed in the nucleus.
the telomeres and ribosomal genes are organized in a non‐random manner in plant cells, and that this organization is maintained throughout the interphase of the cell cycle.
the ribosomal and telomer DNA sequences in P. sativum are organized in discrete, 2‐D and 3‐D nuclear domains, which are not necessarily associated with each other.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of in‐situ localization and 3‐D microscopy provides a powerful tool for the study of the organization of eukaryotic nuclei.
the use of 3‐D fluorescence microscopy combined with computer processing of images is a useful tool in the analysis of nuclear organization.
3‐D microscopy and in‐situ localization can be used to investigate the organization of DNA sequences in intact cells and tissues.
